extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and parties in inter partes review (IPR) proceedings before the PTAB (attorneys, agents, expert witnesses)
extracted.subtask_description: A Patent Trial and Appeal Board Final Written Decision analyzing patentability (anticipation and obviousness) of challenged claims in an inter partes review, including claim construction, burdens of proof, and application of prior-art combination principles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction and statutory basis for IPR
rubrics_metrics.description: We have jurisdiction to hear this inter partes review under 35 U.S.C. § 6. This Final Written Decision is issued pursuant to 35 U.S.C. § 318(a) and 37 C.F.R. § 42.73.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedural prerequisite: IPRs are governed by these statutory/regulatory provisions; final written decisions dispose of instituted challenges under §318(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof in IPR (preponderance of the evidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: In an [inter partes review], the petitioner has the burden from the onset to show with particularity why the patent it challenges is unpatentable. The burden of proof is on the Petitioner to show that the challenged claims are unpatentable; that burden never shifts to the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petition must identify with particularity the supporting evidence per 35 U.S.C. §312(a)(3). The standard of proof for unpatentability in IPR is preponderance of the evidence (35 U.S.C. §316(e); applicable case law cited).

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard (Phillips / §282(b) standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board applies the same claim construction standard used to construe claim terms in a civil action under 35 U.S.C. § 282(b). Under that standard, claim terms are generally given their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look principally to intrinsic evidence (claim language, written description, prosecution history). Extrinsic evidence is less significant in determining legally operative meaning (Phillips; DePuy Spine; C.R. Bard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic evidence primary; extrinsic less significant
rubrics_metrics.description: In determining the meaning of the disputed claim limitation, we look principally to the intrinsic evidence of record, examining the claim language itself, the written description, and the prosecution history, if in evidence. Extrinsic evidence is 'less significant than the intrinsic record' in determining claim meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give greatest weight to intrinsic sources; use extrinsic (expert testimony, dictionaries) only to assist, not to contradict intrinsic record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition from specification controls when claim term is defined
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the term 'fixed dose' is defined by the Specification and is not disputed by the parties, we determine that this term requires no further construction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If specification expressly defines a claim term, adopt that definition (here: 'fixed dose' = dosage administered without regard to patient weight or BSA, not mg/kg or mg/m2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional claim language can be limiting
rubrics_metrics.description: Functional language is limiting upon an apparatus claim when the functional language informs the structural requirements of the claimed device. e.g., we interpret the claim phrase 'delivers to a patient' as a functional limitation requiring that the claimed device be capable of containing and delivering the dose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not automatically treat functional language as mere intended use; analyze whether the language imposes structural capability requirements (K-2 Corp. cited). But avoid importing additional limitations beyond the claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not import method-of-treatment or unwritten limitations into device claims
rubrics_metrics.description: We decline to adopt Patent Owner’s construction that would require the device to 'safely and effectively deliver' the amount of drug to patients with IL-6-mediated disorders, because to do so would impermissibly extend the scope of the claims beyond their language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only read into the claim what the claim language and intrinsic evidence support; avoid adding substantive limitations that relate to patient condition or efficacy unless expressly recited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of 'delivers to a patient' in this case
rubrics_metrics.description: We construe the claim phrase 'delivers to a patient' as a functional limitation of the claims that requires that the claimed device be capable of subcutaneously delivering the dose contained within it to a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This construction does not limit 'patient' to persons with a particular disease nor require demonstrable safe/effective treatment outcomes; it requires capability to deliver subcutaneously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'contains and delivers' / single-device delivery not required
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim language does not require that the fixed dose be administered in a single injection; the claims require only that the device be capable of containing and delivering the fixed dose. The term 'dose' is temporal ('to be taken at one time') and need not imply a single injection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not construe 'contains and delivers' to mandate single-injection delivery absent specific claim or clear intrinsic support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation standard (single reference, express or inherent)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference. A reference can anticipate even if it 'does not expressly spell out' all limitations, if a POSA reading it would 'at once envisage' the claimed arrangement or combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a single prior-art reference discloses all claim elements either explicitly or inherently; inherent disclosure must necessarily be present in the reference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness (Graham factors) and burden for obviousness
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 if differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a POSA. Resolve obviousness using factual determinations: (1) scope and content of prior art; (2) differences between claimed subject matter and prior art; (3) level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioner must show obviousness by a preponderance of the evidence; use KSR and related precedent to inform analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine / reasonable expectation of success
rubrics_metrics.description: When all elements are found in various pieces of prior art, the factfinder must consider whether a POSA would be motivated to combine those references and whether the POSA would have had a reasonable expectation of success. Both the suggestion and expectation of success must be founded in the prior art, not in the applicant’s disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for explicit or implicit teachings in the prior art that provide motivation and reasonable likelihood of success; avoid relying on hindsight or the patentee's disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: KSR 'obvious to try' / predictable solutions guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: When there is a design need or market pressure to solve a problem and there are a finite number of identified, predictable solutions, a POSA has good reason to pursue known options; if this leads to anticipated success, it may be obvious under §103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Obviousness may be shown by a combination that would have been obvious to try with a reasonable expectation of success, particularly where solutions are predictable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Level of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Level of skill in the art is a factual determination important to obviousness. In this case the Board adopted the Decision to Institute definition: an individual with an M.D. specializing in treatment of autoimmune disorders with several years experience researching treatments for autoimmune disorders (including RA); or an individual with M.D. and/or Ph.D. with several years experience, having access to individuals skilled in clinical medicine, pharmacokinetics, and formulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The prior art itself can reflect the appropriate level of ordinary skill (Okajima); parties' expert testimony and inventors' backgrounds inform POSITA definition, but Board will adopt definition consistent with record and prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication / public accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether a reference qualifies as a 'printed publication' is a legal conclusion based on underlying factual findings, including whether the reference was publicly accessible. Evidence such as witness testimony about a website's public accessibility and the site's design/purpose can support a finding of public accessibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish public accessibility with credible factual evidence (e.g., witness familiarity, contemporaneous descriptions of a public website like ClinicalTrials.gov); Board assesses witness credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and credibility of expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: We have reviewed the credentials of Petitioner’s and Patent Owner’s declarants and consider them each to be qualified to provide the opinions for which their testimony has been submitted. The Board credits or discounts expert testimony based on its reasoning, factual basis, and consistency with the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert opinions must address the relevant factual and technical issues; credibility affects evidentiary weight in claim construction, public accessibility, and technical questions such as formulation/viscosity issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficacy or safety not required for apparatus claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Independent claims directed to an article of manufacture (a device) are not limited by any requirement for a showing of the efficacy or safety of administering the drug; the claims are apparatus claims and whether the dose delivered is efficacious is immaterial to the apparatus claim's scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not require clinical efficacy data for anticipation/obviousness of device claims unless efficacy or safety is expressly recited in the claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic evidence over prosecut ion history and specification (avoid overreaching)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not impermissibly extend the scope of the claims through claim construction beyond the language of the claims. For example, requiring that the patient be in need of treatment or importing consideration of immunogenicity/comfort absent claim language is improper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit construction to what is supported by claim language and intrinsic record; prosecution history may inform meaning but cannot add new substantive claim limitations without clear support.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation by implication / inherent disclosure nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference can anticipate if it inherently discloses the claimed subject matter even if not expressly spelled out, but the inherent disclosure must necessarily be present and would be recognized by a POSA reading the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully evaluate whether alleged inherent properties are necessarily present in the prior art reference rather than being merely possible or speculative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prior-art combination to address technical problems
rubrics_metrics.description: When prior art references teach complementary aspects (e.g., clinical use of a dose, a delivery device for similar biologics, and a formulation enabling high concentration), a POSA may be motivated to combine them to achieve claimed subject matter if the prior art provides reasonable expectation of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the teachings of each reference, whether they are analogous, whether a POSA would have been motivated to combine, and whether combination yields predictable success rather than requiring inventive skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural disposition of evidentiary motions where claims resolved
rubrics_metrics.description: Because we find that Petitioner has established that claims 1–8 are unpatentable, we dismiss Petitioner’s Motion to Exclude Evidence as moot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Board resolves dispositive issues on the merits, some subsidiary evidentiary motions may be rendered moot; parties should be aware of potential mootness outcomes.
